Summary & Tips

4-Month Totals:
  • ~200 problems solved (5E/7M/3H per pattern avg)
  • 20 patterns fully covered with theory + practice
  • ~400 hours invested (3.5 hrs/day × 120 days)
  • Weekly revision built into every week's Day 7
Daily Schedule Template (3-4 hrs):
  • 30 min — Theory/pattern review + templates
  • 90 min — Solve 2-3 new problems (timed: 20-30 min each)
  • 30 min — Study optimal solutions for problems you couldn't solve
  • 30 min — Revisit 1-2 old problems from previous weeks
Rules to follow:
  • If stuck for 20 min, look at hints. If stuck for 30 min, study the solution — don't waste time
  • Always write time/space complexity after solving
  • Maintain a "redo list" — problems you got wrong, revisit every Sunday
  • Week 4, 8, 12, 16 = review weeks — no new patterns, just consolidation
  • Track your solve rate: target 70%+ without hints by Month 3

JavaScript Prerequisites for DSA

Before diving into patterns, master these JS fundamentals that appear constantly in DSA problem solving.

Loops and Iteration

// === FOR LOOP (most common in DSA) ===
for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) { }          // standard forward
for (let i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) { }     // reverse iteration
for (let i = 0; i < n; i += 2) { }      // step by 2
for (let i = start; i < end; i++) { }   // range iteration

// Nested loops (brute force, 2D grids)
for (let i = 0; i < rows; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < cols; j++) {
        grid[i][j]; // access cell
    }
}

// === FOR...OF (iterate VALUES — arrays, strings, sets, maps) ===
for (const char of "hello") { }        // each character
for (const num of arr) { }              // each element
for (const [key, val] of map) { }       // Map entries
for (const item of set) { }             // Set values

// === FOR...IN (iterate KEYS — objects only, avoid for arrays) ===
for (const key in obj) {
    if (obj.hasOwnProperty(key)) { }   // skip inherited props
}
// ⚠️ NEVER use for...in on arrays — order not guaranteed, includes prototype

// === WHILE (unknown iterations, pointer movement, BFS) ===
while (left < right) { }                // two pointers
while (queue.length > 0) { }            // BFS processing
while (node !== null) { }               // linked list traversal
while (n > 0) { n = n >> 1; }           // bit processing

// === DO...WHILE (execute at least once, then check) ===
do {
    slow = slow.next;
    fast = fast.next.next;
} while (slow !== fast);                 // cycle detection

// === CONTROL FLOW inside loops ===
break;      // exit loop entirely
continue;   // skip to next iteration
return;     // exit entire function (common in recursion)

// Labeled break (rare, but useful for nested loops)
outer: for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < m; j++) {
        if (found) break outer;            // breaks both loops
    }
}
When to use which loop:
  • for (i) — when you need index access, specific start/end, or step control
  • for...of — when you just need values (cleaner for strings, sets, maps)
  • while — when termination condition isn't index-based (pointers, BFS, linked lists)
  • do...while — rare; when first iteration must always execute (cycle detection)
  • forEach — avoid in DSA (can't break/return early from it)

Variables and Scope

// let — block-scoped, reassignable (use for loop counters, pointers, accumulators)
let left = 0, right = arr.length - 1;
let count = 0;
let maxSoFar = -Infinity;

// const — block-scoped, NOT reassignable (use for everything else)
const result = [];           // array itself can't be reassigned, but contents CAN change
const map = new Map();      // same — you can .set() on it
const n = nums.length;      // value won't change

// var — function-scoped, AVOID in modern JS (hoisting causes bugs)
// Only encounter it in legacy code

// Rule of thumb for DSA:
// • const by default
// • let only when the value WILL be reassigned
// • never var

Conditionals and Ternary

// Standard if/else
if (condition) { } else if (other) { } else { }

// Ternary — compact conditional assignment (very common in DSA)
const val = condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse;
const dir = dx === 0 ? 'horizontal' : 'vertical';

// Nested ternary (use sparingly)
const sign = n > 0 ? 1 : n < 0 ? -1 : 0;

// Logical operators as conditionals
node && node.left;           // short-circuit — safe access
val || defaultVal;           // fallback for falsy
val ?? defaultVal;           // fallback for null/undefined ONLY

// Optional chaining (safe deep access)
node?.left?.val;             // undefined if any part is null/undefined

// Switch (useful for state machines, direction arrays)
switch (dir) {
    case 'up':    row--; break;
    case 'down':  row++; break;
    case 'left':  col--; break;
    case 'right': col++; break;
}

Array Methods

// Mutating methods
arr.push(4);           // add to end → returns new length
arr.pop();              // remove from end → returns removed
arr.unshift(0);        // add to front → returns new length
arr.shift();            // remove from front → returns removed
arr.splice(i, 1);      // remove 1 element at index i (in-place)
arr.splice(i, 0, x);   // insert x at index i
arr.sort((a, b) => a - b);  // numeric ascending sort (in-place)
arr.reverse();          // reverse in-place
arr.fill(0);             // fill all elements with 0

// Non-mutating methods
arr.slice(start, end); // sub-array [start, end) — does NOT modify original
arr.concat(arr2);      // merge arrays
arr.includes(val);     // boolean check
arr.indexOf(val);      // first index or -1
arr.lastIndexOf(val);  // last index or -1
arr.join('');           // array → string
arr.flat(Infinity);    // flatten nested arrays

// Higher-order (used heavily in DSA)
arr.map(x => x * 2);          // transform each element
arr.filter(x => x > 0);        // keep elements passing test
arr.reduce((acc, x) => acc + x, 0); // accumulate to single value
arr.every(x => x > 0);         // true if ALL pass
arr.some(x => x > 0);          // true if ANY passes
arr.find(x => x > 5);          // first element passing test
arr.findIndex(x => x > 5);     // first index passing test

// Creating arrays
const zeros = new Array(5).fill(0);           // [0,0,0,0,0]
const grid = Array.from({length: n}, () => new Array(m).fill(0)); // n×m matrix
const range = Array.from({length: n}, (_, i) => i); // [0,1,...,n-1]

String Methods

str.split('');            // string → array of chars
str.split(' ');           // split by spaces → words
str.charAt(i);           // char at index (or str[i])
str.charCodeAt(i);       // ASCII/Unicode value
String.fromCharCode(97); // → 'a'
str.substring(i, j);     // sub-string [i, j)
str.slice(i, j);          // same but supports negative indices
str.toLowerCase();        // for case-insensitive compare
str.toUpperCase();
str.trim();               // remove leading/trailing whitespace
str.repeat(n);            // repeat n times
str.startsWith('abc');
str.endsWith('xyz');
str.includes('sub');
str.replace(/regex/g, 'new'); // replace all matches
str.match(/regex/g);       // array of all matches

// Key insight: strings are IMMUTABLE in JS
// To modify, convert to array → modify → join back
let chars = str.split('');
chars[0] = 'X';
str = chars.join('');

Map and Set

// Map — ordered key-value store (any type as key)
const map = new Map();
map.set(key, value);
map.get(key);            // undefined if not found
map.has(key);            // boolean
map.delete(key);
map.size;                // number of entries
map.clear();
for (const [k, v] of map) { }  // iterate
map.keys();  map.values();  map.entries();

// Frequency counter pattern (VERY common)
const freq = new Map();
for (const ch of str) {
    freq.set(ch, (freq.get(ch) || 0) + 1);
}

// Set — unique values only
const set = new Set();
set.add(val);
set.has(val);            // O(1) lookup
set.delete(val);
set.size;
[...set];                // convert to array
new Set(arr);            // deduplicate array

// Object as hashmap (only string/symbol keys)
const obj = {};
obj[key] = val;
delete obj[key];
key in obj;              // check existence
Object.keys(obj);       // array of keys
Object.values(obj);     // array of values
Object.entries(obj);    // [[key, val], ...]

Stack and Queue in JS

// Stack — use array (LIFO)
const stack = [];
stack.push(item);        // O(1)
stack.pop();              // O(1)
stack[stack.length - 1]; // peek top
stack.length === 0;      // isEmpty

// Queue — array works for small sizes
const queue = [];
queue.push(item);        // enqueue — O(1)
queue.shift();            // dequeue — O(n) ⚠️
queue[0];                // peek front

// For BFS with large data, use index-based queue (avoids O(n) shift)
let front = 0;
const q = [];
q.push(item);             // enqueue
const val = q[front++];   // dequeue O(1)
front < q.length;         // hasMore

// Deque (double-ended queue) — use array
const deque = [];
deque.push(x);      // add to back
deque.pop();         // remove from back
deque.unshift(x);   // add to front
deque.shift();       // remove from front

Sorting and Comparators

// Default sort is LEXICOGRAPHIC (strings) — always provide comparator for numbers!
[10, 9, 2, 1].sort();          // [1, 10, 2, 9] — WRONG for numbers
[10, 9, 2, 1].sort((a, b) => a - b); // [1, 2, 9, 10] — ascending
[10, 9, 2, 1].sort((a, b) => b - a); // [10, 9, 2, 1] — descending

// Sort by custom key
intervals.sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]);    // sort by first element
words.sort((a, b) => a.length - b.length); // sort by length

// Multi-key sort
arr.sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0] || a[1] - b[1]);

// String sort (locale-aware)
words.sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b));

Math Utilities

Math.max(...arr);         // max of array (spread for arrays)
Math.min(...arr);
Math.abs(x);
Math.floor(x);            // round down
Math.ceil(x);             // round up
Math.round(x);
Math.trunc(x);            // remove decimal (towards zero)
Math.pow(base, exp);      // or use base ** exp
Math.sqrt(x);
Math.log2(x);             // useful for binary tree height

// Integer division (no // operator in JS)
Math.floor(a / b);        // positive numbers
Math.trunc(a / b);        // works for negative too (towards zero)
(a / b) | 0;             // bitwise trick (32-bit only)

// Infinity
let min = Infinity;       // for tracking minimum
let max = -Infinity;      // for tracking maximum

// Modulo (for large numbers, cyclic patterns)
((a % m) + m) % m;        // correct modulo for negative numbers

Destructuring and Spread

// Array destructuring — swap without temp variable
[a, b] = [b, a];

// Spread operator
const copy = [...arr];          // shallow copy array
const merged = [...arr1, ...arr2];
Math.max(...arr);               // spread into function args

// Rest parameters
const [first, ...rest] = arr;  // first element + remaining

// Object spread (for cloning state in DP/backtracking)
const clone = { ...obj };
const updated = { ...obj, key: newVal };

Bitwise Operations

// Essential bitwise ops for DSA
x & y;       // AND
x | y;       // OR
x ^ y;       // XOR (very common — find unique element)
~x;          // NOT
x << n;      // left shift (multiply by 2^n)
x >> n;      // right shift (divide by 2^n)
x >>> n;     // unsigned right shift

// Common tricks
x & 1;        // check if odd (1 = odd, 0 = even)
x & (x - 1); // remove lowest set bit
x | (x + 1); // set lowest unset bit
n >> 1;       // integer divide by 2
1 << n;       // 2^n

// Count set bits
function countBits(n) {
    let count = 0;
    while (n) { n &= (n - 1); count++; }
    return count;
}

Reference vs Value

// Primitives are passed by VALUE (number, string, boolean)
let a = 5;
let b = a;   // b is a COPY — changing b won't affect a

// Objects/Arrays are passed by REFERENCE
let arr1 = [1, 2, 3];
let arr2 = arr1;      // arr2 points to SAME array
arr2.push(4);          // arr1 is also modified!

// To get a real copy:
const copy = [...arr];          // shallow copy
const deep = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)); // deep copy (no functions/symbols)
const deep2 = structuredClone(obj);  // modern deep copy

// IMPORTANT for backtracking:
result.push([...current]); // push a COPY, not the reference
// If you push `current` directly, later modifications affect stored result!

Closures and Recursion State

// Closure pattern for backtracking — variables declared outside are shared
function solve(nums) {
    const result = [];   // shared via closure
    const path = [];

    function backtrack(start) {
        result.push([...path]); // snapshot current path
        for (let i = start; i < nums.length; i++) {
            path.push(nums[i]);    // choose
            backtrack(i + 1);     // explore
            path.pop();             // un-choose (backtrack)
        }
    }

    backtrack(0);
    return result;
}

// Memoization with closures
function memoize(fn) {
    const cache = new Map();
    return function(...args) {
        const key = args.join(',');
        if (cache.has(key)) return cache.get(key);
        const result = fn.apply(this, args);
        cache.set(key, result);
        return result;
    };
}

Linked List Node and Tree Node

// Linked List node (used in many problems)
class ListNode {
    constructor(val = 0, next = null) {
        this.val = val;
        this.next = next;
    }
}

// Binary Tree node
class TreeNode {
    constructor(val = 0, left = null, right = null) {
        this.val = val;
        this.left = left;
        this.right = right;
    }
}

// Graph representation
// Adjacency list (most common)
const graph = new Map();
for (const [u, v] of edges) {
    if (!graph.has(u)) graph.set(u, []);
    if (!graph.has(v)) graph.set(v, []);
    graph.get(u).push(v);
    graph.get(v).push(u); // undirected
}

// Adjacency list with array (when nodes are 0 to n-1)
const adj = Array.from({length: n}, () => []);
for (const [u, v] of edges) {
    adj[u].push(v);
    adj[v].push(u);
}

1 Two Pointers

Concept & Theory

What is it? The Two Pointers technique uses two pointers (indices) that move through a data structure (usually a sorted array or linked list) simultaneously, either towards each other, away from each other, or in the same direction at different speeds.

Why does it work? When an array is sorted, the relationship between elements at two positions gives us information about whether we need to move left or right. This eliminates the need for nested loops, reducing O(n²) to O(n).

Core Idea: Instead of brute-forcing all pairs (i,j), we intelligently skip impossible pairs by leveraging the sorted order. If arr[left] + arr[right] is too small, moving left forward increases the sum. If too large, moving right backward decreases it.

Types of Two Pointer approaches:

  • Opposite Direction (Converging): One pointer starts at beginning, other at end. They move toward each other. Used for: pair sum, palindrome check, container with most water.
  • Same Direction (Fast-Slow or Read-Write): Both start at beginning. One moves faster. Used for: removing duplicates, partitioning arrays, squaring sorted array.
  • Two Arrays: One pointer per array. Used for: merging sorted arrays, intersection of arrays.

Time Complexity: O(n) — each pointer traverses the array at most once.

Space Complexity: O(1) — only two variables regardless of input size.

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Problem involves a sorted array or linked list and you need to find pairs/triplets
  • You need to find a set of elements that satisfy certain constraints (sum = target)
  • Problem says "in-place" — remove/move elements without extra space
  • Comparing elements from both ends (palindrome, container problems)
  • Keywords: "pair", "triplet", "sorted array", "two sum", "in-place", "remove duplicates"
  • When brute force would be O(n²) with nested loops over a sorted structure

Hints & Shortcuts

  • Always sort first (if not already sorted) — Two pointers usually needs sorted input
  • For 3Sum/4Sum: Fix one element, then use two pointers on the rest → reduces by one degree
  • Skip duplicates: After finding a valid pair, skip all identical values: while(left < right && nums[left] === nums[left-1]) left++
  • For "closest to target": Track minimum difference as you traverse
  • Dutch National Flag: Use 3 pointers (low, mid, high) for 3-way partitioning

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ Forgot to sort: Two pointers on unsorted array gives wrong results
  • ⚠️ Duplicate handling: For unique triplets, must skip duplicates at BOTH pointer positions
  • ⚠️ Off-by-one: Use left < right not left <= right (unless you want same element twice)
  • ⚠️ Integer overflow: When summing, use nums[left] + nums[right] vs target not nums[left] vs target - nums[right] in languages with overflow
  • ⚠️ Empty/single element arrays: Always handle edge cases first

Code Snippet to Remember

// Template: Two Sum variant (sorted array)
function twoSumSorted(arr, target) {
    let left = 0, right = arr.length - 1;
    
    while (left < right) {
        const sum = arr[left] + arr[right];
        
        if (sum === target) {
            return [left, right]; // Found pair
        } else if (sum < target) {
            left++;   // Need larger sum → move left forward
        } else {
            right--;  // Need smaller sum → move right backward
        }
    }
    return [-1, -1]; // No pair found
}

// Template: Remove Duplicates In-Place (same direction)
function removeDuplicates(nums) {
    if (nums.length === 0) return 0;
    let writePtr = 1; // slow pointer (write position)
    
    for (let readPtr = 1; readPtr < nums.length; readPtr++) {
        if (nums[readPtr] !== nums[readPtr - 1]) {
            nums[writePtr] = nums[readPtr];
            writePtr++;
        }
    }
    return writePtr; // new length
}

// Template: Three Sum (fix one + two pointers)
function threeSum(nums) {
    nums.sort((a, b) => a - b);
    const result = [];
    
    for (let i = 0; i < nums.length - 2; i++) {
        if (i > 0 && nums[i] === nums[i-1]) continue; // skip duplicates
        let left = i + 1, right = nums.length - 1;
        
        while (left < right) {
            const sum = nums[i] + nums[left] + nums[right];
            if (sum === 0) {
                result.push([nums[i], nums[left], nums[right]]);
                while (left < right && nums[left] === nums[left+1]) left++;
                while (left < right && nums[right] === nums[right-1]) right--;
                left++; right--;
            } else if (sum < 0) left++;
            else right--;
        }
    }
    return result;
}

2 Sliding Window

Concept & Theory

What is it? The Sliding Window pattern maintains a "window" (a contiguous subarray/substring) that expands or shrinks based on conditions. Instead of recalculating everything for each subarray from scratch, you add the new element entering the window and remove the element leaving it.

Why does it work? For contiguous subarray/substring problems, consecutive windows overlap significantly. A window of size k shares k-1 elements with its neighbor. Reusing this overlap eliminates redundant computation.

Two Types:

  • Fixed-size window: Window size is given (find max sum of subarray of size k). Slide one element at a time: add right, remove left.
  • Variable-size (Dynamic) window: Window expands/shrinks based on a condition (smallest subarray with sum ≥ target). Expand right to satisfy condition, then shrink left to optimize.

The Expansion-Contraction Dance:

  1. Start with both pointers at index 0
  2. Expand: Move right pointer → include new element in window state
  3. Check: Is window valid/invalid based on problem constraint?
  4. Contract: Move left pointer → remove element from window state, until window is valid again
  5. Track answer at each valid state

Time Complexity: O(n) — each element is added once and removed once.

Space Complexity: O(1) for fixed window, O(k) for dynamic (hashmap to track window contents).

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Problem asks about contiguous subarrays or substrings
  • Keywords: "maximum/minimum subarray", "longest/shortest substring", "window of size k"
  • Finding longest/shortest something that satisfies a condition
  • Maximum sum/average of subarray of given size
  • String problems with character frequency constraints
  • Anagram finding, permutation in string
  • When brute force would check all O(n²) subarrays

Hints & Shortcuts

  • Fixed window template: Process first k elements, then slide: add arr[i], remove arr[i-k]
  • Variable window "shrink" condition: For "longest" → shrink when INVALID. For "shortest" → shrink when VALID
  • Use a HashMap/frequency counter for substring problems to track character counts in window
  • Track "formed" count: Number of unique characters that meet the desired frequency
  • At most K → Exactly K trick: exactlyK(k) = atMostK(k) - atMostK(k-1)

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ Off-by-one in window size: Window size = right - left + 1, NOT right - left
  • ⚠️ Forgetting to update state when shrinking: When you move left, MUST remove that element from your tracking structure
  • ⚠️ When to update answer: For "longest valid" update INSIDE the valid check. For "shortest valid" update BEFORE shrinking
  • ⚠️ Empty string/array edge cases: What if k > array length? What if no valid window exists?
  • ⚠️ Negative numbers: Sliding window for "sum" doesn't work well with negatives (consider prefix sum instead)

Code Snippet to Remember

// Template: Fixed-Size Sliding Window
function maxSumSubarray(arr, k) {
    let windowSum = 0, maxSum = -Infinity;
    
    for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
        windowSum += arr[i];          // Add incoming element
        
        if (i >= k) {
            windowSum -= arr[i - k];  // Remove outgoing element
        }
        if (i >= k - 1) {
            maxSum = Math.max(maxSum, windowSum); // Window is full
        }
    }
    return maxSum;
}

// Template: Variable-Size Window (Longest valid substring)
function longestSubstringKDistinct(s, k) {
    const charFreq = new Map();
    let left = 0, maxLen = 0;
    
    for (let right = 0; right < s.length; right++) {
        // Expand: add right char to window
        charFreq.set(s[right], (charFreq.get(s[right]) || 0) + 1);
        
        // Shrink: while window is INVALID (more than k distinct)
        while (charFreq.size > k) {
            charFreq.set(s[left], charFreq.get(s[left]) - 1);
            if (charFreq.get(s[left]) === 0) charFreq.delete(s[left]);
            left++;
        }
        
        // Update answer (window is valid here)
        maxLen = Math.max(maxLen, right - left + 1);
    }
    return maxLen;
}

// Template: Shortest/Minimum Window
function minWindowSubstring(s, t) {
    const need = new Map();
    for (const c of t) need.set(c, (need.get(c) || 0) + 1);
    
    let left = 0, formed = 0, minLen = Infinity, minStart = 0;
    const windowCounts = new Map();
    
    for (let right = 0; right < s.length; right++) {
        windowCounts.set(s[right], (windowCounts.get(s[right]) || 0) + 1);
        if (need.has(s[right]) && windowCounts.get(s[right]) === need.get(s[right])) formed++;
        
        // Shrink while window is VALID (has all required chars)
        while (formed === need.size) {
            if (right - left + 1 < minLen) { minLen = right - left + 1; minStart = left; }
            windowCounts.set(s[left], windowCounts.get(s[left]) - 1);
            if (need.has(s[left]) && windowCounts.get(s[left]) < need.get(s[left])) formed--;
            left++;
        }
    }
    return minLen === Infinity ? "" : s.substring(minStart, minStart + minLen);
}

3 Fast & Slow Pointers (Floyd's Cycle Detection)

Concept & Theory

What is it? Also known as the "Tortoise and Hare" algorithm. Two pointers move at different speeds through a sequence. The slow pointer moves 1 step at a time, the fast pointer moves 2 steps. If there's a cycle, they MUST meet. If no cycle, fast reaches the end.

Why does it work mathematically? Imagine a circular track. If one runner is twice as fast, the gap between them decreases by 1 each step. Eventually the gap becomes 0 → they meet. Formally: if cycle length is C, after the slow enters the cycle, they meet within C steps.

Finding the cycle start: After detection, reset one pointer to head. Move both at speed 1. They meet at cycle start. This works because: if the distance from head to cycle start is 'a', and from cycle start to meeting point is 'b', then a = C - b (where C is cycle length).

Beyond cycles - Middle finding: When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle! Fast travels 2x distance, so when fast = end, slow = middle.

Applications:

  • Detecting cycles in linked lists
  • Finding the start of a cycle
  • Finding middle of linked list
  • Detecting cycles in sequences (happy number)
  • Finding duplicate number (array as linked list)

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Problem mentions cycle detection in linked list or sequence
  • Need to find middle element of linked list in one pass
  • Problem involves a circular structure or repeated sequence
  • Keywords: "cycle", "circular", "loop", "middle", "happy number", "duplicate in range [1,n]"
  • When sequence eventually repeats (like squaring digits repeatedly)
  • Can't use extra space (HashSet) for cycle detection

Hints & Shortcuts

  • Middle of list: slow = slow.next, fast = fast.next.next. When fast hits null, slow is middle
  • For even-length lists: Depending on whether fast starts at head or head.next, you get left-middle or right-middle
  • Palindrome linked list: Find middle → reverse second half → compare both halves
  • Rearrange linked list: Find middle → reverse second half → interleave
  • Cycle length: After detection (meeting point), keep one pointer fixed, move other until they meet again. Count steps = cycle length

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ Null check before fast.next: Always check fast !== null && fast.next !== null before moving fast
  • ⚠️ Even vs Odd list length: For middle, behavior differs. Test with both 4 and 5 nodes
  • ⚠️ Single node / empty list: Edge case — return immediately
  • ⚠️ Meeting ≠ Cycle start: Meeting point is NOT necessarily where the cycle begins. Need second phase
  • ⚠️ Infinite loop: If you forget the null checks, fast pointer dereferences null

Code Snippet to Remember

// Template: Cycle Detection in Linked List
function hasCycle(head) {
    let slow = head, fast = head;
    
    while (fast !== null && fast.next !== null) {
        slow = slow.next;          // 1 step
        fast = fast.next.next;     // 2 steps
        if (slow === fast) return true; // They met → cycle exists
    }
    return false; // Fast reached end → no cycle
}

// Template: Find Cycle Start
function detectCycleStart(head) {
    let slow = head, fast = head;
    
    while (fast && fast.next) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
        if (slow === fast) { // Cycle detected
            slow = head;   // Reset slow to head
            while (slow !== fast) { // Both move at speed 1
                slow = slow.next;
                fast = fast.next;
            }
            return slow; // Cycle start node
        }
    }
    return null;
}

// Template: Find Middle of Linked List
function findMiddle(head) {
    let slow = head, fast = head;
    while (fast && fast.next) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
    }
    return slow; // Middle node (right-middle for even length)
}

// Template: Happy Number (cycle in number sequence)
function isHappy(n) {
    const getNext = (num) => {
        let sum = 0;
        while (num > 0) { sum += (num % 10) ** 2; num = Math.floor(num / 10); }
        return sum;
    };
    let slow = n, fast = getNext(n);
    while (fast !== 1 && slow !== fast) {
        slow = getNext(slow);
        fast = getNext(getNext(fast));
    }
    return fast === 1;
}

4 Merge Intervals

Concept & Theory

What is it? The Merge Intervals pattern deals with overlapping intervals. An interval is a pair [start, end]. Two intervals overlap if one starts before the other ends. The pattern involves sorting intervals by start time, then processing them sequentially to merge, insert, or find intersections.

Core Logic: After sorting by start time, for consecutive intervals A and B: if A.end >= B.start → they overlap → merge into [A.start, max(A.end, B.end)]. Otherwise, they're disjoint.

Key Insight: After sorting, you only need to compare each interval with the PREVIOUS one (or the last merged result). No need to check all pairs.

Variations:

  • Merge overlapping: Combine all overlapping intervals into one
  • Insert interval: Add new interval and merge if needed
  • Interval intersection: Find overlap between two lists of intervals
  • Meeting rooms: Can a person attend all meetings? (check any overlap)
  • Minimum meeting rooms: Maximum overlapping intervals at any point

Time Complexity: O(n log n) for sorting + O(n) for merging = O(n log n)

Space Complexity: O(n) for the result array (O(log n) for sort)

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Problem involves intervals, ranges, or time periods
  • Need to find overlaps, gaps, or merge ranges
  • Keywords: "intervals", "meetings", "overlapping", "merge", "schedule", "booking"
  • Given list of [start, end] pairs
  • Problems about scheduling, calendar conflicts, free time
  • Need to find how many events happen simultaneously

Hints & Shortcuts

  • Always sort by start first: This is step 1 in almost every interval problem
  • Overlap condition: a.start <= b.end && b.start <= a.end (bidirectional check)
  • After sorting: Simpler check: current.start <= prev.end
  • Min meeting rooms = max concurrent events: Use a min-heap of end times, or sweep line technique
  • Sweep Line shortcut: Create events: +1 at start, -1 at end. Sort all events. Running sum = concurrent count

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ Sort by start, break ties by end: If starts are equal, shorter interval first (or longer, depending on problem)
  • ⚠️ Contained intervals: [1,10] contains [2,5]. After merge: [1,10]. Don't just extend end blindly — use max()
  • ⚠️ Insert interval: Don't modify the original array. Build result array in 3 parts: before, merged, after
  • ⚠️ Meeting rooms II: Sort by start. Use min-heap of end times. If new meeting starts after earliest end → reuse room (pop+push). Else → new room (push). Heap size = rooms needed
  • ⚠️ Boundary touching: Is [1,5],[5,8] overlapping? Depends on problem. Clarify inclusive vs exclusive boundaries

Code Snippet to Remember

// Template: Merge Overlapping Intervals
function mergeIntervals(intervals) {
    if (intervals.length <= 1) return intervals;
    intervals.sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]); // Sort by start
    
    const merged = [intervals[0]];
    
    for (let i = 1; i < intervals.length; i++) {
        const last = merged[merged.length - 1];
        const curr = intervals[i];
        
        if (curr[0] <= last[1]) {  // Overlapping
            last[1] = Math.max(last[1], curr[1]); // Extend end
        } else {
            merged.push(curr);  // No overlap, add new
        }
    }
    return merged;
}

// Template: Insert Interval
function insertInterval(intervals, newInterval) {
    const result = [];
    let i = 0;
    
    // Add all intervals that come BEFORE newInterval
    while (i < intervals.length && intervals[i][1] < newInterval[0]) {
        result.push(intervals[i++]);
    }
    // Merge all overlapping intervals with newInterval
    while (i < intervals.length && intervals[i][0] <= newInterval[1]) {
        newInterval[0] = Math.min(newInterval[0], intervals[i][0]);
        newInterval[1] = Math.max(newInterval[1], intervals[i][1]);
        i++;
    }
    result.push(newInterval);
    // Add remaining intervals
    while (i < intervals.length) result.push(intervals[i++]);
    return result;
}

// Template: Meeting Rooms II (min rooms needed)
function minMeetingRooms(intervals) {
    const starts = intervals.map(i => i[0]).sort((a,b) => a-b);
    const ends = intervals.map(i => i[1]).sort((a,b) => a-b);
    let rooms = 0, endPtr = 0;
    
    for (let i = 0; i < starts.length; i++) {
        if (starts[i] < ends[endPtr]) rooms++;
        else endPtr++;
    }
    return rooms;
}

5 Cyclic Sort

Concept & Theory

What is it? Cyclic Sort is an in-place sorting algorithm specifically for arrays containing numbers in a given range (1 to n, or 0 to n). The key insight: if numbers are in range [1, n], then number 'i' should be at index 'i-1'. We iterate and swap each number to its correct position.

Why is it special? It sorts in O(n) time and O(1) space — better than comparison sorts! But it only works when numbers are from a known continuous range.

Algorithm:

  1. Start at index i = 0
  2. If nums[i] is not at its correct position (nums[i] ≠ i+1), swap it to where it belongs: swap(nums[i], nums[nums[i]-1])
  3. Keep swapping at current index until the correct number is placed here (or duplicate found)
  4. Move to next index

After sorting: Any index where nums[i] ≠ i+1 tells us something is missing or duplicated!

Time Complexity: O(n) — each number is swapped at most once to its correct position.

Space Complexity: O(1) — all swaps are in-place.

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Array contains numbers in range [1, n] or [0, n]
  • Need to find missing number(s) or duplicate number(s)
  • Keywords: "missing number", "find duplicate", "numbers from 1 to n", "first missing positive"
  • Asked to solve in O(n) time and O(1) space
  • Array length is n and values are bounded by n
  • Problems that say "contains numbers from 1 to n with some missing/duplicated"

Hints & Shortcuts

  • Correct position formula: For range [1,n]: number x goes to index x-1. For range [0,n]: number x goes to index x
  • While loop, not if: Keep swapping at same index until correct number lands there
  • Finding missing: After cyclic sort, scan array. Where nums[i] ≠ i+1, that number (i+1) is missing
  • Finding duplicate: After cyclic sort, where nums[i] ≠ i+1, nums[i] is the duplicate
  • Skip invalid numbers: If number is out of range [1,n] or already in correct position, skip

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ Infinite loop with duplicates: Must check nums[i] !== nums[nums[i]-1] before swapping (not just nums[i] !== i+1)
  • ⚠️ Index calculation: For 1-indexed range: correct index = nums[i] - 1. Don't forget the -1
  • ⚠️ Out of range values: Skip numbers ≤ 0 or > n (they can't be placed correctly)
  • ⚠️ Don't increment i during swaps: Only increment when current position has correct value
  • ⚠️ First Missing Positive is tricky: First filter to only care about numbers in [1, n], then apply cyclic sort

Code Snippet to Remember

// Template: Cyclic Sort (numbers 1 to n)
function cyclicSort(nums) {
    let i = 0;
    while (i < nums.length) {
        const correctIdx = nums[i] - 1; // Where this number should be
        if (nums[i] !== nums[correctIdx]) {
            [nums[i], nums[correctIdx]] = [nums[correctIdx], nums[i]]; // Swap
        } else {
            i++; // Correct position or duplicate, move on
        }
    }
    return nums;
}

// Template: Find Missing Number (range 0 to n)
function missingNumber(nums) {
    let i = 0;
    const n = nums.length;
    while (i < n) {
        const correctIdx = nums[i];
        if (nums[i] < n && nums[i] !== nums[correctIdx]) {
            [nums[i], nums[correctIdx]] = [nums[correctIdx], nums[i]];
        } else { i++; }
    }
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (nums[i] !== i) return i;
    }
    return n;
}

// Template: Find All Duplicates
function findDuplicates(nums) {
    let i = 0;
    while (i < nums.length) {
        const correctIdx = nums[i] - 1;
        if (nums[i] !== nums[correctIdx]) {
            [nums[i], nums[correctIdx]] = [nums[correctIdx], nums[i]];
        } else { i++; }
    }
    const duplicates = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        if (nums[i] !== i + 1) duplicates.push(nums[i]);
    }
    return duplicates;
}

// Template: First Missing Positive
function firstMissingPositive(nums) {
    const n = nums.length;
    let i = 0;
    while (i < n) {
        const correctIdx = nums[i] - 1;
        // Only swap if in valid range and not already correct
        if (nums[i] > 0 && nums[i] <= n && nums[i] !== nums[correctIdx]) {
            [nums[i], nums[correctIdx]] = [nums[correctIdx], nums[i]];
        } else { i++; }
    }
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (nums[i] !== i + 1) return i + 1;
    }
    return n + 1;
}

6 In-place Reversal of Linked List

Concept & Theory

What is it? This pattern reverses a linked list (or part of it) by changing the direction of node pointers in-place, without using extra space. The fundamental operation: make each node point to its previous node instead of its next node.

The Three-Pointer Technique: You need three references at all times:

  • prev: The previous node (starts as null, becomes new head after reversal)
  • current: The node being processed (pointer will be reversed)
  • next: Save the next node BEFORE you reverse current's pointer (otherwise you lose the rest of the list)

Step by step for each node:

  1. Save next: next = current.next
  2. Reverse pointer: current.next = prev
  3. Move prev forward: prev = current
  4. Move current forward: current = next

Variants:

  • Reverse entire list: prev starts at null, iterate until current is null
  • Reverse sub-list (between positions m and n): Navigate to position m, reverse n-m+1 nodes, reconnect
  • Reverse in groups of k: Reverse k nodes, connect to next group, repeat
  • Reverse alternating k-groups: Reverse k, skip k, repeat

Time Complexity: O(n) single pass. Space: O(1) in-place.

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Problem asks to reverse a linked list or part of it
  • Need to reverse nodes between positions m and n
  • Reverse in groups of k
  • Keywords: "reverse", "linked list", "in-place", "group of k"
  • When you need the list in opposite order without extra space
  • Palindrome check on linked list (reverse second half)

Hints & Shortcuts

  • Always save next FIRST: Before changing any pointer, save current.next
  • Dummy node trick: For sub-list reversal, use a dummy head to simplify edge cases
  • Sub-list reversal connections: Save the node before sub-list (lastNodeOfFirstPart) and first node of sub-list (which becomes last after reversal)
  • Recursive reversal: Base case: null or single node. Recurse on rest, then reverse pointer
  • Count first for k-groups: Count remaining nodes before attempting reversal to handle last group < k

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ Losing reference: If you reverse current.next without saving next, you lose the rest of the list
  • ⚠️ Return value: After full reversal, new head is prev (not current, which is null)
  • ⚠️ Sub-list reconnection: After reversing middle section, must connect: part1.end → reversed.start AND reversed.end → part3.start
  • ⚠️ Reverse k-group last part: If remaining nodes < k, leave them as-is (don't reverse)
  • ⚠️ Off-by-one in positions: "Reverse from position 2 to 4" — count carefully, 1-indexed

Code Snippet to Remember

// Template: Reverse Entire Linked List
function reverseList(head) {
    let prev = null, current = head;
    
    while (current !== null) {
        const next = current.next; // 1. Save next
        current.next = prev;       // 2. Reverse pointer
        prev = current;            // 3. Move prev forward
        current = next;            // 4. Move current forward
    }
    return prev; // New head
}

// Template: Reverse Sub-list (between positions m and n, 1-indexed)
function reverseBetween(head, m, n) {
    if (m === n) return head;
    
    const dummy = { next: head };
    let prev = dummy;
    
    // Move to node before position m
    for (let i = 0; i < m - 1; i++) prev = prev.next;
    
    let current = prev.next; // First node to reverse
    const tail = current;    // This will be tail of reversed section
    let reversedPrev = null;
    
    // Reverse n - m + 1 nodes
    for (let i = 0; i < n - m + 1; i++) {
        const next = current.next;
        current.next = reversedPrev;
        reversedPrev = current;
        current = next;
    }
    
    // Connect: prev → reversed head, reversed tail → remaining
    prev.next = reversedPrev;
    tail.next = current;
    
    return dummy.next;
}

// Template: Reverse in K-Groups
function reverseKGroup(head, k) {
    // Count if we have k nodes
    let count = 0, node = head;
    while (node && count < k) { node = node.next; count++; }
    if (count < k) return head; // Less than k nodes, don't reverse
    
    // Reverse k nodes
    let prev = null, current = head;
    for (let i = 0; i < k; i++) {
        const next = current.next;
        current.next = prev;
        prev = current;
        current = next;
    }
    
    // head is now tail of reversed group, connect to next group
    head.next = reverseKGroup(current, k);
    return prev; // New head of this group
}

7 Tree BFS (Breadth-First Search / Level Order Traversal)

Concept & Theory

What is it? BFS explores a tree level by level using a queue. All nodes at depth d are processed before any node at depth d+1. This naturally gives us "level order" traversal — processing siblings before children.

How the Queue works:

  1. Start: Push root into queue
  2. Process level: Note queue size (= nodes at this level). Process exactly that many nodes.
  3. For each node processed: add its children to queue (they'll be processed in the NEXT level)
  4. Repeat until queue is empty

Why track level size? The queue at any point contains nodes from at most 2 consecutive levels. By recording queue.length at the start of each level, we know exactly how many nodes belong to the current level.

Key Properties:

  • Finds shortest path in unweighted graphs/trees
  • Processes nodes in order of distance from root
  • Space: O(w) where w = maximum width of tree (worst case O(n/2) for complete tree's last level)
  • Time: O(n) — visits every node exactly once

Variants: Level averages, zigzag traversal, right side view, level-end markers, connect level-order siblings, minimum depth.

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Problem asks to traverse tree level by level
  • Need shortest path/minimum depth in a tree
  • Keywords: "level order", "breadth first", "layer by layer", "minimum depth", "right view", "zigzag"
  • Need to process all nodes at same depth together
  • Connect nodes at the same level (next pointers)
  • Find average/sum/max at each level

Hints & Shortcuts

  • Level size trick: const levelSize = queue.length at start of while loop, then process exactly levelSize nodes
  • Right side view: Last node in each level (or first node if traversing right-to-left)
  • Zigzag: Alternate between pushing to front/back of level result array
  • Minimum depth: First leaf node you encounter in BFS = minimum depth (BFS guarantees it)
  • Use array as queue in JS: shift() is O(n). For performance, use index pointer or actual Queue class

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ Empty tree: Always check if (!root) return [] first
  • ⚠️ Queue performance in JS: Array.shift() is O(n). For large trees, use a pointer: let front = 0; queue[front++]
  • ⚠️ Zigzag direction: Use a boolean flag that flips each level, or check level number % 2
  • ⚠️ Don't confuse BFS with DFS: BFS uses Queue (FIFO), DFS uses Stack (LIFO) or recursion
  • ⚠️ Connect next pointers: Process left-to-right, connect each node to next in queue (or null for last in level)

Code Snippet to Remember

// Template: Level Order Traversal
function levelOrder(root) {
    if (!root) return [];
    const result = [];
    const queue = [root];
    
    while (queue.length > 0) {
        const levelSize = queue.length; // Nodes at this level
        const currentLevel = [];
        
        for (let i = 0; i < levelSize; i++) {
            const node = queue.shift();
            currentLevel.push(node.val);
            if (node.left) queue.push(node.left);
            if (node.right) queue.push(node.right);
        }
        result.push(currentLevel);
    }
    return result;
}

// Template: Zigzag Level Order
function zigzagLevelOrder(root) {
    if (!root) return [];
    const result = [];
    const queue = [root];
    let leftToRight = true;
    
    while (queue.length) {
        const levelSize = queue.length;
        const level = [];
        for (let i = 0; i < levelSize; i++) {
            const node = queue.shift();
            leftToRight ? level.push(node.val) : level.unshift(node.val);
            if (node.left) queue.push(node.left);
            if (node.right) queue.push(node.right);
        }
        result.push(level);
        leftToRight = !leftToRight;
    }
    return result;
}

// Template: Minimum Depth (BFS is optimal here)
function minDepth(root) {
    if (!root) return 0;
    const queue = [root];
    let depth = 1;
    
    while (queue.length) {
        const levelSize = queue.length;
        for (let i = 0; i < levelSize; i++) {
            const node = queue.shift();
            if (!node.left && !node.right) return depth; // First leaf!
            if (node.left) queue.push(node.left);
            if (node.right) queue.push(node.right);
        }
        depth++;
    }
}

8 Tree DFS (Depth-First Search)

Concept & Theory

What is it? DFS explores a tree by going as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking. Uses recursion (implicit stack) or explicit stack. Three traversal orders:

  • Pre-order (Root → Left → Right): Process node, then children. Used for: serialization, copying tree, prefix expressions
  • In-order (Left → Root → Right): Process left subtree first. For BST, gives sorted order! Used for: BST validation, kth smallest
  • Post-order (Left → Right → Root): Process children before parent. Used for: calculating heights, deletion, postfix expressions

Recursive DFS template: The power of DFS comes from the call stack naturally handling backtracking. Each recursive call processes a subtree, and the return value "bubbles up" information from children to parent.

Key Patterns within DFS:

  • Top-down: Pass information FROM parent TO children (via parameters). Example: path sum — pass running sum down
  • Bottom-up: Get information FROM children, combine at parent (via return values). Example: tree height — get height of subtrees, return max+1
  • Path tracking: Maintain current path, add node on entry, remove on backtrack

Time: O(n). Space: O(h) where h = height (O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed)

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Need to traverse all paths from root to leaves
  • Problem involves tree height, depth, or diameter
  • Need to validate BST properties
  • Keywords: "path sum", "root to leaf", "maximum depth", "diameter", "subtree", "ancestor"
  • When answer depends on information from subtrees (bottom-up)
  • When you need to explore all possibilities (backtracking on tree)

Hints & Shortcuts

  • Base case: Always if (!node) return ... (null check is your base case)
  • BST in-order = sorted: Use this for kth smallest, validate BST, convert to sorted array
  • Diameter: At each node, diameter through that node = leftHeight + rightHeight. Track global max
  • Path sum: Pass remainingSum down. At leaf: check if remainingSum === 0
  • LCA (Lowest Common Ancestor): If left subtree has one target and right has other, current node is LCA

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ Leaf vs null: A leaf is a node with NO children. !node.left && !node.right. Don't confuse with null
  • ⚠️ Global vs local state: Use closure variable or pass-by-reference for tracking global max/min across recursive calls
  • ⚠️ Path tracking backtrack: If using array to track path, path.push() on entry and path.pop() after both recursive calls
  • ⚠️ BST validation range: Must pass BOTH min and max bounds. Don't just compare with parent
  • ⚠️ Diameter ≠ height: Diameter might not pass through root. Track it as global max across all nodes

Code Snippet to Remember

// Template: Path Sum (Top-Down DFS)
function hasPathSum(root, targetSum) {
    if (!root) return false;
    if (!root.left && !root.right) return targetSum === root.val; // Leaf check
    return hasPathSum(root.left, targetSum - root.val) ||
           hasPathSum(root.right, targetSum - root.val);
}

// Template: Maximum Depth (Bottom-Up DFS)
function maxDepth(root) {
    if (!root) return 0;
    return 1 + Math.max(maxDepth(root.left), maxDepth(root.right));
}

// Template: Diameter of Binary Tree
function diameterOfBinaryTree(root) {
    let maxDiameter = 0;
    
    function height(node) {
        if (!node) return 0;
        const leftH = height(node.left);
        const rightH = height(node.right);
        maxDiameter = Math.max(maxDiameter, leftH + rightH); // Diameter at this node
        return 1 + Math.max(leftH, rightH); // Return height
    }
    
    height(root);
    return maxDiameter;
}

// Template: All Root-to-Leaf Paths
function allPaths(root) {
    const result = [];
    
    function dfs(node, path) {
        if (!node) return;
        path.push(node.val);
        
        if (!node.left && !node.right) {
            result.push([...path]); // Copy path at leaf
        } else {
            dfs(node.left, path);
            dfs(node.right, path);
        }
        path.pop(); // Backtrack!
    }
    
    dfs(root, []);
    return result;
}

// Template: Validate BST
function isValidBST(root, min = -Infinity, max = Infinity) {
    if (!root) return true;
    if (root.val <= min || root.val >= max) return false;
    return isValidBST(root.left, min, root.val) &&
           isValidBST(root.right, root.val, max);
}

9 Two Heaps

Concept & Theory

What is it? The Two Heaps pattern uses a Max-Heap and a Min-Heap together to efficiently find the median of a data stream or manage elements where you need quick access to both the smallest and largest elements in separate halves.

Core Idea for Median:

  • Max-Heap (left half): Stores the smaller half of numbers. Top = largest of the small numbers
  • Min-Heap (right half): Stores the larger half of numbers. Top = smallest of the large numbers
  • Median = maxHeap.top() (odd count) or (maxHeap.top() + minHeap.top()) / 2 (even count)

Balancing Rules:

  1. maxHeap.size should equal minHeap.size (even total) or be exactly 1 more (odd total)
  2. Every element in maxHeap ≤ every element in minHeap
  3. When adding: if num ≤ maxHeap.top → add to maxHeap, else add to minHeap. Then rebalance

Why two heaps? A single sorted structure gives O(n) insertion. Two heaps give O(log n) insertion and O(1) median access.

Time: O(log n) per insert, O(1) for median. Space: O(n)

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Need to find median from a data stream
  • Problem involves maintaining two halves of data with quick access to boundary elements
  • Keywords: "median", "data stream", "middle element", "sliding window median"
  • Need the kth largest AND (n-k)th smallest simultaneously
  • Scheduling problems where you need both earliest deadline and latest start time
  • Problems requiring quick access to both max and min of separate partitions

Hints & Shortcuts

  • JS doesn't have built-in heap: Use a simple array-based implementation or negate values for max-heap
  • Max-Heap trick: Store negative values in a min-heap → acts as max-heap
  • Always add to maxHeap first: Then move maxHeap top to minHeap if needed. Simplifies logic
  • Rebalance after every operation: If sizes differ by more than 1, move top from larger to smaller
  • Sliding window median: Same idea but also need to handle removal (use lazy deletion or balanced BST)

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ Heap property vs sorted: Heap only guarantees root is min/max. Other elements are NOT sorted
  • ⚠️ Balancing after removal: When removing from sliding window, must rebalance heaps
  • ⚠️ Integer overflow in median: Use (a + b) / 2.0 not (a + b) / 2 for floating point median
  • ⚠️ Empty heap checks: Always check heap size before accessing top
  • ⚠️ Negation for max-heap: Remember to negate BACK when reading the value!

Code Snippet to Remember

// Simple MinHeap implementation for JS
class MinHeap {
    constructor() { this.heap = []; }
    size() { return this.heap.length; }
    peek() { return this.heap[0]; }
    push(val) { this.heap.push(val); this._bubbleUp(); }
    pop() {
        const top = this.heap[0];
        const last = this.heap.pop();
        if (this.heap.length) { this.heap[0] = last; this._sinkDown(); }
        return top;
    }
    _bubbleUp() {
        let i = this.heap.length - 1;
        while (i > 0) {
            const parent = Math.floor((i - 1) / 2);
            if (this.heap[i] >= this.heap[parent]) break;
            [this.heap[i], this.heap[parent]] = [this.heap[parent], this.heap[i]];
            i = parent;
        }
    }
    _sinkDown() {
        let i = 0;
        while (2 * i + 1 < this.heap.length) {
            let smallest = 2 * i + 1;
            if (smallest + 1 < this.heap.length && this.heap[smallest+1] < this.heap[smallest]) smallest++;
            if (this.heap[i] <= this.heap[smallest]) break;
            [this.heap[i], this.heap[smallest]] = [this.heap[smallest], this.heap[i]];
            i = smallest;
        }
    }
}

// Template: Find Median from Data Stream
class MedianFinder {
    constructor() {
        this.maxHeap = new MinHeap(); // Store negatives for max-heap
        this.minHeap = new MinHeap();
    }
    
    addNum(num) {
        // Add to maxHeap (left half) - store negated
        this.maxHeap.push(-num);
        
        // Ensure maxHeap's max <= minHeap's min
        this.minHeap.push(-this.maxHeap.pop());
        
        // Balance sizes: maxHeap can have at most 1 extra
        if (this.minHeap.size() > this.maxHeap.size()) {
            this.maxHeap.push(-this.minHeap.pop());
        }
    }
    
    findMedian() {
        if (this.maxHeap.size() > this.minHeap.size()) {
            return -this.maxHeap.peek(); // Odd count
        }
        return (-this.maxHeap.peek() + this.minHeap.peek()) / 2; // Even count
    }
}

10 Subsets / Backtracking

Concept & Theory

What is it? Backtracking is a systematic way to explore ALL possible solutions by building candidates incrementally and abandoning ("backtracking") a candidate as soon as it's determined that it cannot lead to a valid solution.

Think of it as a Decision Tree: At each step, you make a choice (include/exclude an element, place a queen, pick a number). Each choice branches the tree. You explore branches depth-first, undoing choices when you hit a dead end.

The Backtracking Template:

  1. Choose: Make a choice (add element to current path)
  2. Explore: Recurse with the choice made
  3. Un-choose: Remove the choice (backtrack) to try next option

Subsets vs Permutations vs Combinations:

  • Subsets: All possible subsets. At each element: include or exclude. 2^n subsets total
  • Permutations: All orderings. At each position: try each unused element. n! permutations
  • Combinations: Choose k from n without order. Like subsets but with size constraint

Pruning: Skip branches that can't lead to valid solutions. This is what makes backtracking efficient. Without pruning, it's just brute force.

Time: O(2^n) for subsets, O(n!) for permutations. Space: O(n) recursion depth

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Need to find ALL possible solutions (not just count or optimal)
  • Keywords: "all subsets", "all permutations", "all combinations", "generate all", "N-Queens"
  • Problem involves choosing from a set with constraints
  • Constraint satisfaction problems (Sudoku, word search, crossword)
  • Combinatorial optimization where you must explore possibilities
  • Problems where choices affect future available choices

Hints & Shortcuts

  • Subsets use startIndex: To avoid duplicates, only consider elements at or after startIndex
  • Permutations use visited array: Track which elements are already used in current permutation
  • Handle duplicates: Sort first, then skip: if (i > start && nums[i] === nums[i-1]) continue
  • Collect answer at leaf vs all nodes: Subsets → collect at every node. Combinations → collect only when size = k
  • Pruning conditions: If remaining elements can't possibly satisfy constraint, return early

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ Must copy path when storing: Use result.push([...path]) not result.push(path) (reference vs copy!)
  • ⚠️ Duplicate handling: Must sort array first AND skip same elements at same recursion level
  • ⚠️ Backtrack = undo: Every push() must have a corresponding pop() after recursion
  • ⚠️ Start index for subsets/combinations: Next recursive call uses i+1 (not start+1)
  • ⚠️ Combination Sum (reuse allowed): Pass i (not i+1) to allow reusing same element

Code Snippet to Remember

// Template: All Subsets
function subsets(nums) {
    const result = [];
    
    function backtrack(start, path) {
        result.push([...path]); // Every node is a valid subset
        
        for (let i = start; i < nums.length; i++) {
            path.push(nums[i]);       // Choose
            backtrack(i + 1, path);   // Explore
            path.pop();               // Un-choose (backtrack)
        }
    }
    
    backtrack(0, []);
    return result;
}

// Template: Permutations
function permute(nums) {
    const result = [];
    const used = new Array(nums.length).fill(false);
    
    function backtrack(path) {
        if (path.length === nums.length) {
            result.push([...path]);
            return;
        }
        for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            if (used[i]) continue;
            used[i] = true;
            path.push(nums[i]);
            backtrack(path);
            path.pop();
            used[i] = false;
        }
    }
    
    backtrack([]);
    return result;
}

// Template: Combination Sum (can reuse elements)
function combinationSum(candidates, target) {
    const result = [];
    candidates.sort((a, b) => a - b);
    
    function backtrack(start, path, remaining) {
        if (remaining === 0) { result.push([...path]); return; }
        
        for (let i = start; i < candidates.length; i++) {
            if (candidates[i] > remaining) break; // Pruning!
            path.push(candidates[i]);
            backtrack(i, path, remaining - candidates[i]); // i (not i+1) = can reuse
            path.pop();
        }
    }
    
    backtrack(0, [], target);
    return result;
}

11 Modified Binary Search

Concept & Theory

What is it? Binary Search divides the search space in half each iteration, achieving O(log n). The "modified" version applies this principle to non-obvious scenarios: rotated arrays, finding boundaries (first/last occurrence), searching in 2D matrices, and searching on answer space.

Standard Binary Search Logic:

  1. Define search space: left = 0, right = n-1
  2. Find mid = left + Math.floor((right - left) / 2) — avoids overflow
  3. Compare target with arr[mid]: if equal → found. If target < mid → search left half. If target > mid → search right half
  4. If left > right → not found

Modified Variants:

  • First/Last occurrence: Don't stop at first match. Continue searching in left/right half
  • Rotated sorted array: One half is always sorted. Determine which half, check if target is in that half
  • Search space on answers: Binary search on the answer (not array index). Example: minimum capacity to ship packages in D days
  • 2D matrix: Treat as 1D array: row = mid / cols, col = mid % cols
  • Peak element: If mid > mid+1, peak is on left side (including mid). Else right side

Time: O(log n). Space: O(1)

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Sorted array (or partially sorted like rotated)
  • Keywords: "sorted", "search", "O(log n)", "rotated", "first/last position", "peak"
  • Problem asks for minimum/maximum that satisfies a condition (binary search on answer)
  • The search space can be halved based on some condition
  • Finding boundary/transition point (from false to true)
  • Optimization problems: "minimum capacity", "maximum distance", "split array"

Hints & Shortcuts

  • Use left + (right - left) / 2: Prevents integer overflow (matters in some languages)
  • Left boundary (first occurrence): When found, set right = mid - 1, keep searching left. Answer is left after loop
  • Right boundary (last occurrence): When found, set left = mid + 1, keep searching right. Answer is right after loop
  • Rotated array: Check which half is sorted by comparing arr[left] vs arr[mid]
  • Binary Search on Answer: Define a canAchieve(mid) function. If can achieve with mid → try smaller. If can't → try larger

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ Infinite loop: Ensure left or right ALWAYS changes. Use left = mid + 1 and right = mid - 1 (not right = mid)
  • ⚠️ While condition: left <= right for standard search, left < right for boundary finding (depends on template)
  • ⚠️ Off-by-one: The most common bug. Test with arrays of size 1, 2 to verify
  • ⚠️ Rotated array with duplicates: When arr[left] === arr[mid] === arr[right], must do left++ (can't determine which half is sorted). Worst case O(n)
  • ⚠️ Floor vs Ceil mid: For even-length arrays, mid biases left. Sometimes you need mid = left + Math.ceil((right - left) / 2)

Code Snippet to Remember

// Template: Standard Binary Search
function binarySearch(arr, target) {
    let left = 0, right = arr.length - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        const mid = left + Math.floor((right - left) / 2);
        if (arr[mid] === target) return mid;
        else if (arr[mid] < target) left = mid + 1;
        else right = mid - 1;
    }
    return -1;
}

// Template: First & Last Position (Lower/Upper Bound)
function firstPosition(arr, target) {
    let left = 0, right = arr.length - 1, result = -1;
    while (left <= right) {
        const mid = left + Math.floor((right - left) / 2);
        if (arr[mid] === target) { result = mid; right = mid - 1; } // Keep searching left
        else if (arr[mid] < target) left = mid + 1;
        else right = mid - 1;
    }
    return result;
}

// Template: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
function searchRotated(nums, target) {
    let left = 0, right = nums.length - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        const mid = left + Math.floor((right - left) / 2);
        if (nums[mid] === target) return mid;
        
        if (nums[left] <= nums[mid]) { // Left half is sorted
            if (target >= nums[left] && target < nums[mid]) right = mid - 1;
            else left = mid + 1;
        } else { // Right half is sorted
            if (target > nums[mid] && target <= nums[right]) left = mid + 1;
            else right = mid - 1;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

// Template: Binary Search on Answer Space
function minCapacityToShip(weights, days) {
    let left = Math.max(...weights); // Min possible capacity
    let right = weights.reduce((a, b) => a + b); // Max capacity (ship all in 1 day)
    
    while (left < right) {
        const mid = left + Math.floor((right - left) / 2);
        if (canShipInDays(weights, mid, days)) right = mid; // Try smaller
        else left = mid + 1; // Need more capacity
    }
    return left;
}

function canShipInDays(weights, capacity, days) {
    let daysNeeded = 1, currentLoad = 0;
    for (const w of weights) {
        if (currentLoad + w > capacity) { daysNeeded++; currentLoad = 0; }
        currentLoad += w;
    }
    return daysNeeded <= days;
}

12 Bitwise XOR

Concept & Theory

What is it? XOR (exclusive or) is a bitwise operation with unique mathematical properties that solve specific problems in O(n) time and O(1) space where other approaches need more.

Key XOR Properties (MEMORIZE THESE!):

  • a ^ 0 = a — XOR with 0 gives the number itself
  • a ^ a = 0 — XOR with itself gives 0 (cancellation!)
  • a ^ b ^ a = b — The duplicate cancels out, leaving the unique one
  • XOR is commutative and associative: order doesn't matter
  • a ^ b = 0 means a === b

Why XOR is powerful: When you XOR all numbers together, duplicates cancel (become 0), and unique numbers survive. This finds single numbers in arrays where every other number appears twice.

Bit Manipulation essentials:

  • n & (n-1) — Clears the lowest set bit (used for counting set bits)
  • n & (-n) — Isolates the lowest set bit (rightmost 1-bit)
  • n >> 1 — Divide by 2 (right shift)
  • n << 1 — Multiply by 2 (left shift)
  • n & 1 — Check if odd (last bit is 1)

Time: O(n). Space: O(1)

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Find the single/unique number where others appear in pairs
  • Find two unique numbers in array where others appear twice
  • Find missing number from a range
  • Keywords: "single number", "appears once", "missing", "without extra space", "bit manipulation"
  • Swapping without temp variable
  • Problems requiring O(1) space that seem to need a set/map

Hints & Shortcuts

  • Single Number: XOR all elements. Pairs cancel, unique remains
  • Missing Number [0,n]: XOR all elements with XOR of [0..n]. Missing number remains
  • Two single numbers: XOR all → gets a^b. Find any set bit (rightmost). Partition numbers by that bit. XOR each group separately
  • Swap without temp: a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b; (but careful with same variable!)
  • Check power of 2: n > 0 && (n & (n-1)) === 0

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ XOR same variable: a ^= a makes a = 0! Never swap a variable with itself using XOR
  • ⚠️ Negative numbers: In JS, bitwise operations work on 32-bit integers. Large numbers may give unexpected results
  • ⚠️ XOR doesn't help with "appears 3 times": For that, use bit counting (sum bits mod 3)
  • ⚠️ Order matters for understanding, not result: XOR is commutative, but tracing through code can be confusing
  • ⚠️ JS bitwise limits: JavaScript converts numbers to 32-bit integers for bitwise ops. Numbers > 2^31 - 1 may behave unexpectedly

Code Snippet to Remember

// Template: Find Single Number (every other appears twice)
function singleNumber(nums) {
    let result = 0;
    for (const num of nums) {
        result ^= num; // Pairs cancel out, unique remains
    }
    return result;
}

// Template: Find Two Single Numbers (others appear twice)
function twoSingleNumbers(nums) {
    let xorAll = 0;
    for (const n of nums) xorAll ^= n; // xorAll = a ^ b
    
    // Find rightmost set bit (where a and b differ)
    const diffBit = xorAll & (-xorAll);
    
    let group1 = 0, group2 = 0;
    for (const n of nums) {
        if (n & diffBit) group1 ^= n; // Bit set → one group
        else group2 ^= n;              // Bit not set → other group
    }
    return [group1, group2];
}

// Template: Missing Number (range 0 to n)
function missingNumber(nums) {
    let xor = nums.length; // Start with n
    for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        xor ^= i ^ nums[i]; // XOR index and value
    }
    return xor; // Missing number survives
}

// Template: Count Set Bits (Brian Kernighan's Algorithm)
function countBits(n) {
    let count = 0;
    while (n) {
        n &= (n - 1); // Clear lowest set bit
        count++;
    }
    return count;
}

13 Top K Elements

Concept & Theory

What is it? This pattern efficiently finds the K largest/smallest/most frequent elements from a collection using a heap (priority queue). Instead of sorting the entire array (O(n log n)), we maintain a heap of size K (O(n log k)).

Two Approaches:

  • Min-Heap of size K (for K largest): Keep K largest elements. When heap size > K, remove minimum. After processing all elements, heap contains K largest. Top = Kth largest.
  • Max-Heap of size K (for K smallest): Keep K smallest elements. When heap size > K, remove maximum. After processing, heap contains K smallest.

Why Min-Heap for K largest? The min-heap's top is the SMALLEST of the K largest elements (= the Kth largest). Any element smaller than heap's top cannot be in top-K, so we skip/remove it.

QuickSelect Alternative: For finding just the Kth element (not all K), QuickSelect gives O(n) average time. Uses partition logic from QuickSort.

Frequency-based Top K: First count frequencies with a HashMap, then use heap on the frequency values. Or use Bucket Sort for O(n).

Time: O(n log k) with heap. O(n) average with QuickSelect. Space: O(k) for heap

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Find the K largest, smallest, or most frequent elements
  • Keywords: "top K", "Kth largest", "K most frequent", "K closest", "K pairs"
  • Need elements sorted by some custom criteria and only need top K
  • Streaming data — can't sort everything, maintain running top-K
  • When K is much smaller than n (heap approach is better than full sort)
  • Finding K elements closest to a target value or point

Hints & Shortcuts

  • K largest → use Min-Heap of size K: Counterintuitive but correct! The min lets you evict the smallest of the K candidates
  • K smallest → use Max-Heap of size K: Evict the largest of the K candidates
  • Bucket Sort for frequency: Create array of size n+1. Index = frequency. O(n) time!
  • For K closest points: Use max-heap with distance as key. If new point closer than heap top, replace
  • QuickSelect partition: Pick pivot, partition around it. If pivot is at index k-1, found! If left of k, search right. If right of k, search left

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ Heap size check: Only pop when heap size EXCEEDS K (push first, then check)
  • ⚠️ Kth largest vs K largest: Kth largest = one element. K largest = set of K elements. Same heap approach works for both
  • ⚠️ Custom comparator: For complex objects (points, words), define proper comparison function
  • ⚠️ QuickSelect worst case: O(n²) if pivot is always min/max. Use random pivot for O(n) average
  • ⚠️ Tie handling in frequency: If two elements have same frequency, clarify which comes first (alphabetical? first seen?)

Code Snippet to Remember

// Template: Kth Largest Element using Min-Heap
function findKthLargest(nums, k) {
    const minHeap = new MinHeap(); // Use MinHeap class from Pattern 9
    
    for (const num of nums) {
        minHeap.push(num);
        if (minHeap.size() > k) {
            minHeap.pop(); // Remove smallest, keep K largest
        }
    }
    return minHeap.peek(); // Top of min-heap = Kth largest
}

// Template: Top K Frequent Elements (Bucket Sort - O(n))
function topKFrequent(nums, k) {
    const freqMap = new Map();
    for (const n of nums) freqMap.set(n, (freqMap.get(n) || 0) + 1);
    
    // Bucket: index = frequency, value = list of numbers with that frequency
    const buckets = Array.from({length: nums.length + 1}, () => []);
    for (const [num, freq] of freqMap) {
        buckets[freq].push(num);
    }
    
    // Collect from highest frequency bucket downward
    const result = [];
    for (let i = buckets.length - 1; i >= 0 && result.length < k; i--) {
        result.push(...buckets[i]);
    }
    return result.slice(0, k);
}

// Template: K Closest Points to Origin
function kClosest(points, k) {
    // Sort by distance (or use heap for better performance)
    points.sort((a, b) => (a[0]**2 + a[1]**2) - (b[0]**2 + b[1]**2));
    return points.slice(0, k);
}

// Template: QuickSelect for Kth Largest (O(n) average)
function quickSelect(nums, k) {
    const target = nums.length - k; // Kth largest = (n-k)th in sorted order
    
    function partition(left, right) {
        const pivot = nums[right];
        let i = left;
        for (let j = left; j < right; j++) {
            if (nums[j] <= pivot) {
                [nums[i], nums[j]] = [nums[j], nums[i]];
                i++;
            }
        }
        [nums[i], nums[right]] = [nums[right], nums[i]];
        return i;
    }
    
    let left = 0, right = nums.length - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        const pivotIdx = partition(left, right);
        if (pivotIdx === target) return nums[pivotIdx];
        else if (pivotIdx < target) left = pivotIdx + 1;
        else right = pivotIdx - 1;
    }
}

14 K-way Merge

Concept & Theory

What is it? K-way Merge efficiently merges K sorted arrays/lists into one sorted output using a min-heap. Instead of merging pairs repeatedly (K-1 merge passes), we use a heap to always pick the globally smallest element across all K lists.

Algorithm:

  1. Insert the first element of each of the K lists into a min-heap (along with list index and element index)
  2. Pop the minimum element from the heap → add to result
  3. If the popped element's list has more elements, push the next element from that list
  4. Repeat until heap is empty

Why it works: The heap always contains at most K elements (one from each list). The minimum of these K elements is the global minimum of all remaining elements (since each list is sorted).

Comparison with other approaches:

  • Merge all into one array & sort: O(N log N) where N = total elements. Doesn't use sorted property
  • Merge pairs iteratively: O(N log K) but more complex to implement
  • K-way merge with heap: O(N log K) — optimal! Heap operations are O(log K) and done N times

Time: O(N log K) where N = total elements. Space: O(K) for heap

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Merge K sorted arrays/lists/streams
  • Find smallest range covering elements from K lists
  • Keywords: "K sorted", "merge sorted", "K lists", "smallest range", "Kth smallest in matrix"
  • Problems involving multiple sorted inputs that need to be combined
  • Finding Kth smallest element in a sorted matrix
  • External sorting (when data doesn't fit in memory)

Hints & Shortcuts

  • Heap entries need metadata: Store [value, listIndex, elementIndex] to know where to get next element
  • Sorted Matrix Kth smallest: Treat each row (or column) as a sorted list, apply K-way merge until you pop K elements
  • Smallest range: Track max element in heap. Range = [heap.top, currentMax]. Minimize this range
  • Merge K linked lists: Push all head nodes into heap. Pop min, advance that list's pointer, push next
  • Divide & Conquer alternative: Merge lists in pairs, like merge sort. Gives same O(N log K)

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ Empty lists: Some of the K lists might be empty. Skip them when initializing heap
  • ⚠️ Heap comparator: Compare by VALUE, not by list index. Common mistake in custom heap
  • ⚠️ Next element check: Before pushing next element from a list, check if that list has more elements
  • ⚠️ Sorted Matrix: Both rows AND columns are sorted. Can treat as K sorted rows OR use binary search approach
  • ⚠️ K = 1: Edge case — just return the single list as-is

Code Snippet to Remember

// Template: Merge K Sorted Lists
function mergeKLists(lists) {
    const minHeap = new MinHeap(); // Stores [val, listIdx, nodeRef]
    
    // Initialize: add head of each list
    for (let i = 0; i < lists.length; i++) {
        if (lists[i]) minHeap.push([lists[i].val, i, lists[i]]);
    }
    
    const dummy = { next: null };
    let tail = dummy;
    
    while (minHeap.size() > 0) {
        const [val, listIdx, node] = minHeap.pop();
        tail.next = node;
        tail = tail.next;
        
        if (node.next) {
            minHeap.push([node.next.val, listIdx, node.next]);
        }
    }
    return dummy.next;
}

// Template: Merge K Sorted Arrays
function mergeKArrays(arrays) {
    const minHeap = new MinHeap(); // Compare by value
    const result = [];
    
    // Push first element of each array: [value, arrayIdx, elementIdx]
    for (let i = 0; i < arrays.length; i++) {
        if (arrays[i].length > 0) {
            minHeap.push([arrays[i][0], i, 0]);
        }
    }
    
    while (minHeap.size() > 0) {
        const [val, arrIdx, elemIdx] = minHeap.pop();
        result.push(val);
        
        if (elemIdx + 1 < arrays[arrIdx].length) {
            minHeap.push([arrays[arrIdx][elemIdx + 1], arrIdx, elemIdx + 1]);
        }
    }
    return result;
}

// Template: Kth Smallest in Sorted Matrix
function kthSmallest(matrix, k) {
    const n = matrix.length;
    const minHeap = new MinHeap();
    
    // Add first element of each row
    for (let i = 0; i < Math.min(n, k); i++) {
        minHeap.push([matrix[i][0], i, 0]);
    }
    
    let count = 0;
    while (minHeap.size() > 0) {
        const [val, row, col] = minHeap.pop();
        count++;
        if (count === k) return val;
        if (col + 1 < n) minHeap.push([matrix[row][col+1], row, col+1]);
    }
}
