15 Topological Sort

Concept & Theory

What is it? Topological Sort produces a linear ordering of vertices in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) such that for every directed edge (u → v), u comes before v in the ordering. Think of it as "dependency ordering" — tasks that depend on others come after them.

Real-world analogy: Course prerequisites. If Course B requires Course A, then A must come before B in any valid schedule.

Two algorithms:

  • Kahn's Algorithm (BFS-based): Start with nodes having 0 in-degree (no dependencies). Process them, reduce in-degree of neighbors. When neighbor's in-degree becomes 0, add to queue. If all nodes processed → valid ordering. If not → cycle exists!
  • DFS-based: Do DFS. When a node's DFS completes (all descendants processed), add to result. Reverse the result. Uses recursion and visited states (unvisited, in-progress, done).

Cycle Detection: A topological sort exists if and only if the graph has NO cycles. Kahn's detects cycle when processed count < total nodes. DFS detects cycle when visiting an "in-progress" node.

Time: O(V + E). Space: O(V + E) for adjacency list and in-degree array

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Problems involving dependency ordering
  • Keywords: "course schedule", "prerequisites", "build order", "task scheduling", "alien dictionary"
  • Directed graph where you need a valid processing order
  • Detecting cycles in directed graphs
  • Finding if a valid ordering exists
  • Problems where "X must come before Y"

Hints & Shortcuts

  • Kahn's is easier to implement: BFS with in-degree tracking. Also naturally detects cycles
  • Build adjacency list + in-degree array: First step for any topo sort problem
  • Multiple valid orderings: If multiple nodes have in-degree 0 simultaneously, any order is valid
  • Unique ordering: Only if at every step exactly one node has in-degree 0 (queue always has size 1)
  • Alien Dictionary: Compare adjacent words character by character to extract ordering rules → build graph → topo sort

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ Cycle = no valid topo sort: If processed count != total vertices → cycle exists
  • ⚠️ Disconnected graph: Initialize ALL nodes with in-degree 0 into queue (not just first found)
  • ⚠️ Self-loops: A self-loop is a cycle. Handle explicitly
  • ⚠️ Alien Dictionary edge cases: "abc" vs "ab" → "ab" should come first. If longer word comes first, it's INVALID
  • ⚠️ Multiple valid answers: Most problems accept any valid topological order

Code Snippet to Remember

// Template: Kahn's Algorithm (BFS Topological Sort)
function topologicalSort(numCourses, prerequisites) {
    const adjList = Array.from({length: numCourses}, () => []);
    const inDegree = new Array(numCourses).fill(0);
    
    // Build graph
    for (const [course, prereq] of prerequisites) {
        adjList[prereq].push(course);
        inDegree[course]++;
    }
    
    // Initialize queue with nodes having in-degree 0
    const queue = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < numCourses; i++) {
        if (inDegree[i] === 0) queue.push(i);
    }
    
    const order = [];
    while (queue.length > 0) {
        const node = queue.shift();
        order.push(node);
        
        for (const neighbor of adjList[node]) {
            inDegree[neighbor]--;
            if (inDegree[neighbor] === 0) queue.push(neighbor);
        }
    }
    
    // If all nodes processed → valid order, else → cycle
    return order.length === numCourses ? order : [];
}

// Template: Course Schedule (Can Finish?)
function canFinish(numCourses, prerequisites) {
    return topologicalSort(numCourses, prerequisites).length === numCourses;
}

// Template: DFS-based Topo Sort with Cycle Detection
function topoSortDFS(numNodes, edges) {
    const adj = Array.from({length: numNodes}, () => []);
    for (const [u, v] of edges) adj[u].push(v);
    
    const state = new Array(numNodes).fill(0); // 0=unvisited, 1=in-progress, 2=done
    const result = [];
    
    function dfs(node) {
        if (state[node] === 1) return false; // Cycle!
        if (state[node] === 2) return true;  // Already processed
        
        state[node] = 1; // Mark in-progress
        for (const neighbor of adj[node]) {
            if (!dfs(neighbor)) return false;
        }
        state[node] = 2; // Mark done
        result.push(node); // Add to result (reverse at end)
        return true;
    }
    
    for (let i = 0; i < numNodes; i++) {
        if (!dfs(i)) return []; // Cycle detected
    }
    return result.reverse();
}

16 Union Find (Disjoint Set Union)

Concept & Theory

What is it? Union-Find (also called Disjoint Set Union / DSU) is a data structure that tracks elements partitioned into non-overlapping sets. It supports two operations efficiently:

  • Find(x): Determine which set element x belongs to (returns the "representative" or "root" of the set)
  • Union(x, y): Merge the sets containing x and y into a single set

Implementation with two optimizations:

  • Path Compression (in Find): Make every node on the path point directly to root. Flattens the tree, making future finds O(1)
  • Union by Rank/Size: Always attach smaller tree under root of larger tree. Keeps tree balanced

With both optimizations: Nearly O(1) per operation (actually O(α(n)) — inverse Ackermann, practically constant)

When to use over BFS/DFS?

  • When you need to dynamically add edges and check connectivity
  • When you need to count connected components as edges are added
  • When the graph is given as edge list (not adjacency list)
  • Kruskal's MST algorithm uses Union-Find

Time: O(α(n)) ≈ O(1) per operation. Space: O(n)

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Need to track connected components dynamically
  • Keywords: "connected components", "group", "union", "are they connected?", "redundant connection"
  • Problems involving merging groups/sets
  • Detecting cycles in an undirected graph
  • Kruskal's Minimum Spanning Tree
  • Problems where relationships are transitive (friend of friend = friend)

Hints & Shortcuts

  • Initialize: parent[i] = i (each element is its own set). rank[i] = 0
  • Connected check: find(x) === find(y) → same component
  • Count components: Start with n components. Each successful union reduces count by 1
  • Cycle detection (undirected): Before union(u,v), if find(u) === find(v) → adding edge creates cycle
  • 2D grid: Map (row, col) to a 1D index: row * cols + col

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ Path compression modifies structure: find() has a side effect (updates parent). This is intentional
  • ⚠️ Union-Find for undirected only: For directed graphs, use topological sort or DFS for cycle detection
  • ⚠️ Redundant Connection: The edge that creates a cycle = the first edge where find(u) === find(v)
  • ⚠️ Don't union roots incorrectly: Always union the ROOTS of x and y, not x and y themselves
  • ⚠️ Index mapping: For problems with nodes labeled as strings, map to integers first

Code Snippet to Remember

// Template: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union)
class UnionFind {
    constructor(n) {
        this.parent = Array.from({length: n}, (_, i) => i);
        this.rank = new Array(n).fill(0);
        this.components = n;
    }
    
    find(x) {
        if (this.parent[x] !== x) {
            this.parent[x] = this.find(this.parent[x]); // Path compression
        }
        return this.parent[x];
    }
    
    union(x, y) {
        const rootX = this.find(x), rootY = this.find(y);
        if (rootX === rootY) return false; // Already connected
        
        // Union by rank
        if (this.rank[rootX] < this.rank[rootY]) this.parent[rootX] = rootY;
        else if (this.rank[rootX] > this.rank[rootY]) this.parent[rootY] = rootX;
        else { this.parent[rootY] = rootX; this.rank[rootX]++; }
        
        this.components--;
        return true; // Successfully merged
    }
    
    connected(x, y) { return this.find(x) === this.find(y); }
}

// Template: Number of Connected Components
function countComponents(n, edges) {
    const uf = new UnionFind(n);
    for (const [u, v] of edges) uf.union(u, v);
    return uf.components;
}

// Template: Redundant Connection (find cycle-creating edge)
function findRedundantConnection(edges) {
    const uf = new UnionFind(edges.length + 1);
    for (const [u, v] of edges) {
        if (!uf.union(u, v)) return [u, v]; // Already connected = creates cycle
    }
}

// Template: Number of Islands using Union-Find
function numIslands(grid) {
    const rows = grid.length, cols = grid[0].length;
    const uf = new UnionFind(rows * cols);
    let waterCount = 0;
    
    for (let r = 0; r < rows; r++) {
        for (let c = 0; c < cols; c++) {
            if (grid[r][c] === '0') { waterCount++; continue; }
            const id = r * cols + c;
            if (r + 1 < rows && grid[r+1][c] === '1') uf.union(id, (r+1)*cols+c);
            if (c + 1 < cols && grid[r][c+1] === '1') uf.union(id, r*cols+c+1);
        }
    }
    return uf.components - waterCount;
}

17 Monotonic Stack

Concept & Theory

What is it? A Monotonic Stack maintains elements in either strictly increasing or strictly decreasing order. When a new element violates the monotonic property, we pop elements until the property is restored. This efficiently finds the "next greater/smaller element" for each position.

Two types:

  • Monotonic Decreasing Stack: Elements from bottom to top are decreasing. Used to find "Next Greater Element". When a larger element comes, pop all smaller ones (they found their next greater).
  • Monotonic Increasing Stack: Elements from bottom to top are increasing. Used to find "Next Smaller Element". When a smaller element comes, pop all larger ones.

Key Insight: Each element is pushed once and popped once → O(n) total despite the while loop inside the for loop.

What the stack stores: Usually INDICES (not values), because you need to know the position for calculating distances/areas.

Applications:

  • Next Greater Element (right/left)
  • Next Smaller Element (right/left)
  • Largest Rectangle in Histogram
  • Trapping Rain Water
  • Daily Temperatures
  • Stock Span Problem

Time: O(n). Space: O(n) for stack

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Find the next/previous greater or smaller element for each element
  • Keywords: "next greater", "next smaller", "daily temperatures", "stock span", "histogram", "trapping rain water"
  • Problems involving "looking right/left for first element satisfying a condition"
  • Maximum rectangle problems
  • Problems where brute force would check all elements to the right → O(n²)
  • When you need to process elements and maintain a "visible" set

Hints & Shortcuts

  • Store indices, not values: You can always get the value from the index, but not vice versa
  • Next Greater → Decreasing stack: Stack holds potential "watchers". A new bigger element satisfies all smaller watchers
  • Previous Greater → traverse left to right, check stack top
  • Histogram area: For each bar, area = height × width. Width = distance between previous and next smaller bars
  • Circular array: Process array twice (index % n) to handle wraparound

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ Stack stores indices: Common mistake is storing values. You almost always need positions
  • ⚠️ Default value: If stack is empty when checking, use -1 or n (no next greater exists)
  • ⚠️ Strictly vs non-strictly monotonic: For "next greater" use strict (>). For "next greater or equal" use (>=)
  • ⚠️ Left vs Right: For "previous greater" traverse left→right. For "next greater" also left→right (pop gives answer)
  • ⚠️ Histogram rectangle: Add sentinel value 0 at end to force all elements to pop

Code Snippet to Remember

// Template: Next Greater Element (to the right)
function nextGreaterElement(nums) {
    const n = nums.length;
    const result = new Array(n).fill(-1); // Default: no greater element
    const stack = []; // Stores indices, maintaining decreasing values
    
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        // Pop all elements smaller than current (they found their next greater)
        while (stack.length && nums[stack[stack.length-1]] < nums[i]) {
            result[stack.pop()] = nums[i];
        }
        stack.push(i);
    }
    return result;
}

// Template: Daily Temperatures (days until warmer)
function dailyTemperatures(temps) {
    const n = temps.length;
    const result = new Array(n).fill(0);
    const stack = []; // Decreasing temperature indices
    
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        while (stack.length && temps[stack[stack.length-1]] < temps[i]) {
            const idx = stack.pop();
            result[idx] = i - idx; // Distance to next warmer day
        }
        stack.push(i);
    }
    return result;
}

// Template: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
function largestRectangleArea(heights) {
    const stack = []; // Increasing heights (indices)
    let maxArea = 0;
    heights.push(0); // Sentinel to force final pops
    
    for (let i = 0; i < heights.length; i++) {
        while (stack.length && heights[stack[stack.length-1]] > heights[i]) {
            const h = heights[stack.pop()];
            const w = stack.length ? i - stack[stack.length-1] - 1 : i;
            maxArea = Math.max(maxArea, h * w);
        }
        stack.push(i);
    }
    heights.pop(); // Remove sentinel
    return maxArea;
}

// Template: Next Greater Element (Circular Array)
function nextGreaterCircular(nums) {
    const n = nums.length;
    const result = new Array(n).fill(-1);
    const stack = [];
    
    for (let i = 0; i < 2 * n; i++) { // Process array twice
        while (stack.length && nums[stack[stack.length-1]] < nums[i % n]) {
            result[stack.pop()] = nums[i % n];
        }
        if (i < n) stack.push(i);
    }
    return result;
}

18 Dynamic Programming

Concept & Theory

What is it? Dynamic Programming (DP) solves complex problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems, solving each subproblem once, and storing results to avoid redundant computation. It's essentially "smart recursion with memoization" or "building solutions bottom-up from smaller subproblems."

Two required properties:

  • Optimal Substructure: Optimal solution to the problem contains optimal solutions to subproblems
  • Overlapping Subproblems: Same subproblems are solved multiple times (unlike divide & conquer)

Two approaches:

  • Top-Down (Memoization): Write recursive solution, add cache. Easier to think about but has recursion overhead
  • Bottom-Up (Tabulation): Fill a DP table iteratively from smallest subproblem to largest. Usually faster, no stack overflow risk

The DP Framework (5 steps):

  1. Define state: What does dp[i] represent? (Most important step!)
  2. Find recurrence relation: How does dp[i] relate to previous states?
  3. Define base cases: What are dp[0], dp[1]?
  4. Determine iteration order: Which direction to fill the table?
  5. Optimize space if possible: Often only need previous row/state

Common DP Categories: 1D DP, 2D DP, String DP (LCS, Edit Distance), Knapsack, Interval DP, State Machine DP, Tree DP, Bitmask DP

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Problem asks for count of ways, minimum/maximum, or optimal solution
  • Keywords: "minimum cost", "maximum profit", "number of ways", "longest/shortest", "can you reach", "is it possible"
  • Making choices at each step that affect future options
  • Problem has overlapping subproblems (same calculations repeated)
  • Recursive solution has exponential time complexity (often 2^n or n!)
  • Problems involving sequences, strings, grids, or knapsack-like choices

Hints & Shortcuts

  • Start with recursion: Write brute-force recursive solution first, then add memoization
  • State = what changes between calls: Usually index, remaining capacity, previous choice
  • 1D DP common patterns: dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2] (Fibonacci family), dp[i] = max(dp[j] + ...) for all j < i
  • 2D DP strings: dp[i][j] = answer for s1[0..i] and s2[0..j]
  • Space optimization: If dp[i] only depends on dp[i-1], use two variables instead of array

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ Greedy vs DP: If greedy works, don't use DP. DP is for when greedy fails (choices have future consequences)
  • ⚠️ State definition is everything: Wrong state = wrong solution. Spend time thinking about what dp[i] means
  • ⚠️ Base cases: Most DP bugs are wrong base cases. dp[0] = 0? 1? Think carefully
  • ⚠️ Index off-by-one: For string DP, dp table is usually (n+1) × (m+1) with empty string as base
  • ⚠️ Iteration direction: For bottom-up, ensure all needed sub-states are computed before current state

Code Snippet to Remember

// Template: 0/1 Knapsack
function knapsack(weights, values, capacity) {
    const n = weights.length;
    const dp = Array.from({length: n+1}, () => new Array(capacity+1).fill(0));
    
    for (let i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        for (let w = 0; w <= capacity; w++) {
            dp[i][w] = dp[i-1][w]; // Don't take item i
            if (weights[i-1] <= w) {
                dp[i][w] = Math.max(dp[i][w], dp[i-1][w-weights[i-1]] + values[i-1]);
            }
        }
    }
    return dp[n][capacity];
}

// Template: Longest Common Subsequence (LCS)
function longestCommonSubsequence(text1, text2) {
    const m = text1.length, n = text2.length;
    const dp = Array.from({length: m+1}, () => new Array(n+1).fill(0));
    
    for (let i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
        for (let j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
            if (text1[i-1] === text2[j-1]) dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1;
            else dp[i][j] = Math.max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]);
        }
    }
    return dp[m][n];
}

// Template: Climbing Stairs / Fibonacci family
function climbStairs(n) {
    if (n <= 2) return n;
    let prev2 = 1, prev1 = 2;
    for (let i = 3; i <= n; i++) {
        const curr = prev1 + prev2;
        prev2 = prev1;
        prev1 = curr;
    }
    return prev1;
}

// Template: Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS)
function lengthOfLIS(nums) {
    const dp = new Array(nums.length).fill(1);
    for (let i = 1; i < nums.length; i++) {
        for (let j = 0; j < i; j++) {
            if (nums[j] < nums[i]) dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1);
        }
    }
    return Math.max(...dp);
}

// Template: Coin Change (Unbounded Knapsack)
function coinChange(coins, amount) {
    const dp = new Array(amount + 1).fill(Infinity);
    dp[0] = 0;
    for (let i = 1; i <= amount; i++) {
        for (const coin of coins) {
            if (coin <= i) dp[i] = Math.min(dp[i], dp[i - coin] + 1);
        }
    }
    return dp[amount] === Infinity ? -1 : dp[amount];
}

19 Greedy Algorithms

Concept & Theory

What is it? A Greedy algorithm makes the locally optimal choice at each step, hoping it leads to a globally optimal solution. Unlike DP, greedy doesn't reconsider previous choices — it commits to the best option available NOW.

When does Greedy work? Only when the problem has:

  • Greedy Choice Property: A globally optimal solution can be reached by making locally optimal choices
  • Optimal Substructure: Optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems

How to prove greedy works: Exchange argument — show that swapping any non-greedy choice with the greedy choice doesn't make the solution worse.

Common Greedy Strategies:

  • Sort + process in order: Sort by some criterion, then process greedily (Activity Selection, Job Scheduling)
  • Take maximum/minimum available: Always pick the best remaining option (Fractional Knapsack)
  • Two-pass greedy: Scan left-to-right then right-to-left (Candy problem)
  • Jump/reach greedy: Track the farthest you can reach (Jump Game)

Greedy vs DP: If greedy works, it's simpler and faster. But if a counterexample exists, you need DP. Test with small cases!

Time: Usually O(n log n) for sort + O(n) processing = O(n log n). Space: O(1) to O(n)

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Problem asks for minimum/maximum with a "greedy-friendly" structure
  • Keywords: "minimum number of", "maximum events", "minimum coins (specific denominations)", "jump game"
  • Scheduling/interval problems with clear ordering criteria
  • Problems where sorting + single pass gives optimal answer
  • When each choice is independent (doesn't constrain future choices much)
  • Can prove: "greedy choice is always part of some optimal solution"

Hints & Shortcuts

  • Activity Selection: Sort by END time. Always pick the earliest-ending non-conflicting activity
  • Jump Game: Track farthest reachable index. If current index > farthest → can't reach end
  • Candy/Rating problems: Two-pass: left-to-right ensures right neighbor rule, right-to-left ensures left neighbor rule
  • Huffman Coding: Always merge two smallest frequencies
  • Gas Station: If total gas >= total cost, solution exists. Start from where running sum first becomes non-negative

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ Greedy doesn't always work: 0/1 Knapsack, Coin Change (arbitrary coins), Longest Subsequence — need DP
  • ⚠️ Prove before coding: Find a counterexample where greedy fails. If you can't, it likely works
  • ⚠️ Sorting criterion matters: Sort by end time (not start time) for activity selection
  • ⚠️ Don't confuse with two-pointer: Greedy makes irrevocable choices. Two-pointer explores systematically
  • ⚠️ Coin Change greedy only works for specific denominations: [1,5,10,25] works greedy. [1,3,4] with target 6 doesn't (greedy gives 4+1+1=3 coins, but 3+3=2 coins is optimal)

Code Snippet to Remember

// Template: Jump Game (can reach end?)
function canJump(nums) {
    let farthest = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        if (i > farthest) return false; // Can't reach this index
        farthest = Math.max(farthest, i + nums[i]);
    }
    return true;
}

// Template: Jump Game II (minimum jumps)
function jump(nums) {
    let jumps = 0, currentEnd = 0, farthest = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < nums.length - 1; i++) {
        farthest = Math.max(farthest, i + nums[i]);
        if (i === currentEnd) { // Must jump now
            jumps++;
            currentEnd = farthest;
        }
    }
    return jumps;
}

// Template: Activity Selection (max non-overlapping intervals)
function maxActivities(intervals) {
    intervals.sort((a, b) => a[1] - b[1]); // Sort by END time
    let count = 1, lastEnd = intervals[0][1];
    
    for (let i = 1; i < intervals.length; i++) {
        if (intervals[i][0] >= lastEnd) { // Non-overlapping
            count++;
            lastEnd = intervals[i][1];
        }
    }
    return count;
}

// Template: Gas Station (circular route)
function canCompleteCircuit(gas, cost) {
    let totalSurplus = 0, currentSurplus = 0, startIdx = 0;
    
    for (let i = 0; i < gas.length; i++) {
        totalSurplus += gas[i] - cost[i];
        currentSurplus += gas[i] - cost[i];
        if (currentSurplus < 0) { // Can't start from anywhere before i+1
            startIdx = i + 1;
            currentSurplus = 0;
        }
    }
    return totalSurplus >= 0 ? startIdx : -1;
}

20 Trie (Prefix Tree)

Concept & Theory

What is it? A Trie (pronounced "try") is a tree-like data structure that stores strings character by character. Each node represents a character, and paths from root to marked nodes represent complete words. It enables O(L) search/insert (L = word length) regardless of how many words are stored.

Structure:

  • Root node is empty (represents empty prefix)
  • Each node has up to 26 children (for lowercase English letters)
  • Each node has an isEndOfWord flag marking if a complete word ends here
  • Path from root to any node = a prefix that exists in the stored words

Key Operations:

  • Insert(word): For each character, create child node if missing, traverse down. Mark last node as end-of-word
  • Search(word): Traverse following characters. If all found AND last node is end-of-word → word exists
  • StartsWith(prefix): Traverse following characters. If all found (regardless of isEnd) → prefix exists

Why Trie over HashMap?

  • Efficient prefix search (HashMap can't do this easily)
  • Autocomplete and spell-checking
  • Shared prefixes save space (all words starting with "app" share first 3 nodes)
  • Alphabetical ordering comes naturally (DFS gives sorted words)

Time: O(L) per operation (L = word length). Space: O(N × L × 26) worst case, much less with shared prefixes

Pattern Recognition - When to Use

  • Problems involving prefix matching or autocomplete
  • Keywords: "prefix", "dictionary", "word search", "autocomplete", "spell check", "longest common prefix"
  • Need to search for words with wildcards (like "b.d" matching "bad", "bed")
  • Finding all words with a given prefix efficiently
  • Word Break / Word Search problems (Trie + DFS/backtracking)
  • Maximum XOR problems (binary trie)

Hints & Shortcuts

  • Use object/map for children: In JS, children = {} is simpler than array of 26. Access: node.children[char]
  • Wildcard search: When encountering '.', try ALL children (use DFS/recursion)
  • Word Search II (Boggle): Build trie from dictionary, then DFS on grid using trie for pruning
  • Count words with prefix: Add a count field to each node. Increment on insert, check on prefix query
  • Delete word: Navigate to end, unmark isEnd. If no children, remove nodes bottom-up

Tricks & Gotchas

  • ⚠️ Search vs StartsWith: Search requires isEndOfWord = true at last node. StartsWith doesn't
  • ⚠️ Memory usage: Tries use more memory than hash maps for small dictionaries. Use when prefix operations are needed
  • ⚠️ Case sensitivity: Decide upfront if your trie handles uppercase. Usually convert to lowercase first
  • ⚠️ Don't forget isEndOfWord: Without it, searching "app" in a trie containing only "apple" would wrongly return true
  • ⚠️ Word Search II optimization: Remove words from trie after finding them (prune branches for performance)

Code Snippet to Remember

// Template: Trie Implementation
class TrieNode {
    constructor() {
        this.children = {};
        this.isEnd = false;
    }
}

class Trie {
    constructor() { this.root = new TrieNode(); }
    
    insert(word) {
        let node = this.root;
        for (const char of word) {
            if (!node.children[char]) node.children[char] = new TrieNode();
            node = node.children[char];
        }
        node.isEnd = true;
    }
    
    search(word) {
        const node = this._traverse(word);
        return node !== null && node.isEnd;
    }
    
    startsWith(prefix) {
        return this._traverse(prefix) !== null;
    }
    
    _traverse(str) {
        let node = this.root;
        for (const char of str) {
            if (!node.children[char]) return null;
            node = node.children[char];
        }
        return node;
    }
}

// Template: Search with Wildcards (. matches any char)
function searchWithWildcard(root, word) {
    function dfs(node, i) {
        if (i === word.length) return node.isEnd;
        
        if (word[i] === '.') {
            // Try all children
            for (const child of Object.values(node.children)) {
                if (dfs(child, i + 1)) return true;
            }
            return false;
        }
        
        if (!node.children[word[i]]) return false;
        return dfs(node.children[word[i]], i + 1);
    }
    return dfs(root, 0);
}

// Template: Word Search II (Boggle) using Trie
function findWords(board, words) {
    const trie = new Trie();
    for (const w of words) trie.insert(w);
    
    const result = new Set();
    const rows = board.length, cols = board[0].length;
    
    function dfs(r, c, node, path) {
        if (r < 0 || r >= rows || c < 0 || c >= cols) return;
        const char = board[r][c];
        if (char === '#' || !node.children[char]) return;
        
        node = node.children[char];
        path += char;
        if (node.isEnd) result.add(path);
        
        board[r][c] = '#'; // Mark visited
        dfs(r+1,c,node,path); dfs(r-1,c,node,path);
        dfs(r,c+1,node,path); dfs(r,c-1,node,path);
        board[r][c] = char; // Backtrack
    }
    
    for (let r = 0; r < rows; r++)
        for (let c = 0; c < cols; c++)
            dfs(r, c, trie.root, '');
    
    return [...result];
}
